newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end sharply higher on funds, Brazil.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end sharply higher on funds, Brazil.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended sharply higher as funds bought at least 20 million bushels of soybeans amid rumors Brazil would impose an export tax on soybeans, traders said.

"The big push today was because of the rumor about Brazil imposing a three percent tax on exports," said Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc. "Funds came in and bought 10 million bushels right on the open."
Brazilian crushers and the Brazilian Agricultural Ministry said a export tax on soybeans and products was unlikely and would be rejected by the ministry.

Brazilian crushers, whose profits have been squeezed since the abolition of a tax last year, would benefit because a reinstatement of some sort of tax would discourage exports and make domestic soybeans cheaper and more readily available.
CBOT traders said such a tax would raise the price of Brazilian exports and encourage world buyers to purchase U.S. supplies.
Soybeans closed 25 to 5-1/2 cents per bushel higher with May up 21 at $8.49-1/2.

Commodity funds bought at least 20 million bushels of soybeans on the day which led the market to near-limit gains. Several traders said the funds were positioning themselves for a summer weather market amid some long-range forecasts for a cool, wet planting season.

Gains in new crop months were capped by ideas 1997 soybean acreage would increase. Traders cited reports private analytical firm Sparks Companies pegged 1997 soybean acreage at 65.98 million acres, above USDA's oulook conference estimate for 65.3 million.
They also referred to speculation a wet spring would force farmers to plant soybeans instead of corn. Soybeans can be planted later in the growing season than corn.

News two Cargill Inc processors planned to take downtime also weighed on the soybean market. Cargill's Kansas City plant will be down from May 1 through the end of August and its Norfolk, Va. plant will be down as of April 1. Cargill recently closed its Guntersville, Ala., crushing facility because flooding along the Ohio River had made securing soybeans difficult.

Traders said in the wake of the shutdowns, the drop in crushing rates will decrease demand for soybeans. Processors had been crushing about 30 million bushels of soybeans per week, according to the NOPA weekly crush reports.
Volume was estimated by CBOT at 87,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's actual volume of 86,369 contracts.
Funds were aggressive buyers on the day.
Traders said some locals had sold the higher opening and were forced to cover as funds began to buy.
"In came CIS and FIMAT and all of a sudden, everyone who sold on the open was in trouble," a floor trader said.

On the day, Cargill Investor Services bought at least 10 million bushels May soybeans, Refco Inc bought four million May and 1.5 million July and LFG bought two million each May and July, traders said.
Goldenberg-Hehmeyer sold five million May and Dean Witter sold three million May and one million November.
In options trade, Cargill Investor Services sold 500 May $7.50 puts at 1-3/4 cents and ADM bought 400 May $8.25 calls and sold 400 May $8.50 calls at 11 to 12-1/2 cents.
